newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Offshore project may be behind share rise-NZOG.
newsitem.headline: Offshore project may be behind share rise-NZOG.

text.p: NZ Oil and Gas said on Thurday its planned exploration bid west of the Maui field is the only reason it has for its recent share price rise.
On September 24 the company announced it planned to seek oil west of the offshore Maui field in a major change of direction for the company.
The stock, then trading at 38 cents, dipped to 37 cents on October 9 but then climbed steadily to close at 43 cents on Wednesday.

"It may be that this event is being increasingly recognised by the market, particularly in the context of increased oil prices and buoyant share market activity in the petroleum sector in general," company secretary Gordon Ward said in a response to queries from the market surveillance panel.
But in a separate statement NZOG said it would offer a free one for two options issue to enable the company to raise new debt or equity for developments.
NZOG said it was not aware of any statements having been issued by its officers that may have affected the company's share price but noted that the directors had been considering the options issue.

The directors only decided to go ahead with the issue on Wednesday but had held "private preliminary discussions" on the issue with both the New Zealand and Australian stock exchanges, the company said.
The options will have a term of about five years and will be exercisable between July 1, 1998, and October 31, 2001, at a price expected to be in a range of 55 to 70 cents.
"Directors consider that the value of NZOG's assets more than supports the current share price," Ward said.

In a quarterly progress report to September 30 issued today, NZOG said its share of the output of the onshore Taranaki Ngatoro field was up 100 percent from June at 13,800 barrels of oil. Ngatoro-6 had flowed 200-600 barrels a day in testing and awaited tie-in to the rest of the field.
The company had also just received a 25-year specified term mining permit to replace the interim permit it received to operate in the Kupe field in 1992.
Chairman Tony Radford said two to three initial producer wells were expected to be drilled in the field by the end of 1997.
